subject: Agriculture
title: Weed Competition
description: A quick, practical guide to Weed Competition.

hook.text: Weeds cost global agriculture $100 billion per year. They steal light, water, and nutrients from crops.

buildup.text: A single pigweed plant can produce 500,000 seeds. Miss one, and it colonizes the whole field next year.

discovery.text: Herbicides transformed weed control. Glyphosate (Roundup) let farmers kill weeds without harming resistant crops.

twist.text: Over 50 weed species are now glyphosate-resistant. Palmer amaranth in the US South resists everything.

climax.text: Farmers are returning to tillage, cover crops, and manual weeding as chemical options run out.

punchline.text: Weeds evolve faster than herbicides. The arms race never ends.

quiz.question: How many weed species are now glyphosate-resistant?

details.summary: Weeds compete with crops for sunlight, water, and nutrients, and can slash yields by 30% or more if unchecked. This topic covers weed biology, competitive mechanisms, and integrated management strategies that minimize weed damage sustainably.
details.whyItMatters: Weeds cause more crop loss than insects and diseases combined. Herbicide resistance is growing, making alternative weed management strategies increasingly important.
takeaways: Weeds can produce tens of thousands of seeds per plant that persist for years
Critical weed-free periods exist early in crop growth when competition is most damaging
Integrated management combines cultural, mechanical, and chemical methods

faq.question: How do weeds reduce crop yields?
faq.answer: Weeds compete directly for sunlight by shading crops, absorb soil water that crops need, take up nutrients, and can host crop pests and diseases. Fast-growing weeds during early crop stages cause the most damage to final yields.

faq.question: What is the critical weed-free period?
faq.answer: The critical weed-free period is the window early in a crop's life when weed competition causes the most yield loss. For most crops, keeping fields weed-free for the first 4–6 weeks after emergence protects the majority of yield potential.
